ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Otolaryngology (otology/neurotology) Consultation — Martin Luther

code.originalText: Two-week review and otology consultation with audiometry; diagnoses of Ménière disease and recurrent depression

text.paragraph: Recurrent attacks of spinning vertigo for about three months, lasting hours, with roaring tinnitus, fullness and muffled hearing in the left ear, in a 43-year-old man; the tinnitus persists between attacks. Please confirm the cause, arrange audiometry and any imaging, and advise on preventing attacks and protecting his hearing. [S]

list.item: Does he meet the criteria for Ménière disease, and in which ear?
Could this be vestibular migraine, given his headaches, or another cause such as a vestibular schwannoma or a stroke?
Is MRI needed, and are vestibular function tests or electrocochleography useful?
What maintenance treatment do you recommend: salt and caffeine limits, a diuretic, betahistine?
How should he treat an attack, and what should be done if attacks continue?
What can be done for his hearing, tinnitus and balance between attacks?

text.paragraph: Professor Luther, 43, is seen at the request of Dr. Brandt-Mensah. Over about three months he has had three attacks of spinning vertigo, and one more six days ago, each lasting from about one to six hours, with nausea, and each preceded or accompanied by roaring tinnitus and fullness in the left ear and muffled hearing on that side. Between attacks the left-ear tinnitus continues at a lower level. He does not lose consciousness. No attack has come with headache, light or sound sensitivity, or visual aura; he has dull headaches on some other days, without dizziness, and had head and ear noises in his twenties. No ear discharge, ear surgery, head injury or ototoxic drugs. He drinks three to four cups of coffee a day and beer with dinner, and his diet is salty. He is frightened of an attack while preaching or lecturing. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 (Julian calendar) in Eisleben, into a relatively prosperous mining family; his father, Hans, gave him a good education and intended him for law. [D]

He entered the University of Erfurt in 1501 and became a Master of Arts in 1505; later in 1505, after a vow to St Anna made in a thunderstorm, he entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt against his father's wishes, and he was ordained in 1507. [D]

As a monk, although he made full use of confession, he felt that he was 'a sinner before God with an extremely disturbed conscience', and this anxiety and fear meant that he underwent what he termed Anfechtungen, spiritual trials or temptations, in particular about predestination. [D]

He became professor of the Bible at Wittenberg in 1512 and held the post until his death. He published the Ninety-Five Theses on 31 October 1517, refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, was declared an outlaw, was sheltered at the Wartburg, and returned to Wittenberg on 6 March 1522. [D]
In 1525 he married Katharina von Bora, a former nun; they had six children, two daughters of whom died young. [D]
In May 1521, at the Wartburg, he wrote to Philipp Melanchthon that the Lord had afflicted him with painful constipation, and that he had not slept all night. [D]

In the autumn of 1510, in Bologna, he reported severe headache and whizzing in the ear; from 1523, according to his physician Matthias Ratzeberger, he had regular headaches with fainting spells and vertigo. [D]

From 1526 on he had sporadic attacks of urinary stones, which reminded him of death because of the excruciating pain; the first stone, in 1526, was preceded by headache, heaviness in the head, vertigo and nausea and was passed through the urethra. [D]
On 22 April 1527 (Julian) a severe attack of dizziness forced him to break off a sermon. [D]

On the evening of 6 July 1527 (Julian), when he was 43, he had an attack that began with a roaring tinnitus in his left ear, which increased and seemed to fill the left half of his head, followed by nausea, pallor, coldness and a state of collapse without loss of consciousness; he prayed and believed he would not survive the night. After a night's rest all the symptoms had subsided except the tinnitus, which persisted. His friends Justus Jonas and Johannes Bugenhagen wrote accounts of it. [D]
In the first half of 1527 he was deeply disturbed by disputes with other reformers over the Lord's Supper and suffered severe depression. [D]

Feldmann concluded from Luther's letters and his friends' reports that the attacks with tinnitus and vertigo that began in 1527 were a typical case of Ménière disease of the left ear, more than 330 years before Ménière's description; earlier writers had read them as a psychiatric disorder or as chronic inflammation of the middle ear, and a later Japanese review reads them as chronic suppurative otitis media. [R]

Evers, applying modern criteria to the letters, found that some of his vertigo attacks met the criteria for Ménière disease, that others occurred with headaches meeting the criteria for vestibular migraine, and that his headaches partly met the criteria for migraine; he concluded that vestibular migraine with migraine and Ménière disease is possible but not final. [R]

list.item: Ménière disease of the left ear, definite (H81.02). He meets the AAO-HNS 2020 and Bárány Society criteria for definite Ménière disease: two or more spontaneous attacks of vertigo each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, low- to medium-frequency sensorineural hearing loss documented by audiometry in the left ear, and fluctuating tinnitus and fullness in that ear, not better explained by another vestibular diagnosis. The normal examination between attacks argues against a central cause. Vestibular migraine was considered: he has headaches, but no attack has carried migraine features, so the criteria for vestibular migraine are not met; the two can coexist, and a headache diary will show whether that is so. The asymmetric hearing loss calls for MRI to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. Vestibular function testing and electrocochleography are not needed to make the diagnosis. [S]

Maintenance treatment. Sodium restriction and limiting caffeine and alcohol are reasonable first steps. A diuretic is a guideline option for maintenance; hydrochlorothiazide also lowers urine calcium, which may help his stones, but his sodium should be checked, particularly if an SSRI is started. Betahistine is not FDA approved in the United States and the large BEMED trial found it no better than placebo, so it is not recommended. Vestibular suppressants such as meclizine should be limited to attacks, because regular use slows compensation. [S]

Hearing, tinnitus and balance. Hearing is fluctuating and word recognition is still good; no hearing aid is needed now. If unsteadiness persists between attacks, vestibular rehabilitation helps; it is not useful during an attack. If disabling attacks continue after about three months of these measures, an intratympanic steroid injection is the next step; gentamicin or surgery are reserved for refractory disease. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Brandt-Mensah's intake note, examination and tests (blood count, electrolytes, kidney function, calcium, uric acid and TSH normal) and his attack diary. Audiometry today: left low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss of 40 dB at 250 and 500 Hz and 30 dB at 1000 Hz, 15 to 20 dB above that; right ear normal; word recognition 88 percent left and 100 percent right; type A tympanograms on both sides. [S]

list.item: Sodium 1,500 to 2,300 mg a day, caffeine to about one cup a day, and alcohol limited; keep the attack and headache diary. [S]
Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg each morning, with sodium and potassium in two to four weeks. [S]
No betahistine. [S]
Meclizine only for severe attacks, for no more than three days at a time; sit or lie down at the first warning. [S]
MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium. [S]
Vestibular rehabilitation if unsteadiness persists between attacks. [S]
Repeat audiogram at about three months, and sooner with any change in hearing. [S]
Intratympanic steroid if disabling attacks continue after about three months. [S]
Depression care to continue with Dr. Brandt-Mensah; the attacks and the fear of them feed the low mood. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Brandt-Mensah, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis, the reasons for the MRI, the decision against betahistine and the plan were explained to Professor Luther, who was relieved to have a name for the attacks and agreed to the plan. [S]
Follow-up: Otology review in three months with the repeat audiogram, or sooner if attacks continue or hearing changes. [S]
